name: Rosa Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at SunPath, a small solar panel installer with twelve people. I book the install crews, send quotes, chase invoices and file the safety paperwork for every roof. I use AI every day: it drafts my quote emails and I've set it up to sort the inbox into urgent and not urgent. I love it when a crew finishes early because I planned the route well.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you're still learning. What's hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The technical side, honestly. I can't always tell if a roof survey is complete, and Kofi (the owner) has to check my work more than I'd like. Money isn't a worry: I've been putting money into an index fund since I was 19 and I share a cheap flat, so I've got well over a year saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest. I'd post something like it's still a great tool for small firms, and share how it sorts my inbox. People at SunPath would tease me for being the AI fan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it means my job carries on and I keep being the person who knows the tools. That's a nice place to be. I'd also worry a bit that the hype made a few huge companies rich for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for quotes and routes, and maybe build Kofi a simple dashboard for jobs this month. I'd start an evening course on solar design software, because that's where I'm weakest. And I'd keep the index fund going as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little bored by it, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's scared of AI in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friend Lena (a receptionist at a dentist) to try it for one boring task, like reminder texts. She'd see it saves twenty minutes, not her whole job. AI at SunPath (the solar firm where she works) saves twenty minutes on reminder texts, not my whole job. That usually calms people down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else weighing on you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Solar depends on government grants, and those come and go. If the grant scheme ended, SunPath would have a slow year. That worries me more than AI does, in this picture.

say: AI is still a **great tool** for small firms, even without the hype.
I'd share how it **sorts my inbox** and drafts quotes.
think: My job carries on and I stay the one who **knows the tools**.
The hype may have made **a few companies** rich for nothing.
do: Build Kofi a simple **jobs dashboard** with AI.
Take an evening course on **solar design** software.
Keep paying into the **index fund** as normal.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored** by how little changes.
S0.quote: AI at SunPath (the solar firm where she works) saves twenty minutes on reminder texts, not my whole job.
fieldNote: She is already a **daily AI user** and frames herself as the office expert.
Her real worry here is **government grants** for solar, not AI.
She calms friends by pointing to **one boring task**.

steps.text: Build a monthly jobs dashboard for Kofi using AI
Take an evening course in solar design software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure the gains get shared. If AI does the quotes, the crews and office should get shorter weeks, not just the owner a bigger profit. I'd post that, and I'd mean it about every firm, not just ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my admin job shrinks a lot, but I think I'd survive it at SunPath. I'm the one running the tools, so I'd turn into the person who keeps them working. The worry is I'm junior and still shaky on the technical side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate most of my own paperwork in the first few months, before anyone else suggests it. Then I'd ask Kofi to let me train on site surveys, so I can do the hands-on bit too. I'd also join a local campaign for green jobs training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a small worry in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't automating your own work a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. Someone will automate my paperwork, and I'd rather it was me, so I'm the one who understands it. Like I said, the risk is being junior, so I need the survey skills as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at SunPath would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maureen (who does the accounts part-time) is 58 and hates computers. If the AI does invoices, Kofi might not need her. I'd try to help her learn it, but I don't know if she'd want me to.

say: The gains should be **shared**: shorter weeks for workers, not just **bigger profits**.
Every firm, not only ours, should **share the time** AI saves.
think: My admin job **shrinks a lot**, but I'd become the person running the tools.
Being **junior** and weak on technical work is my real risk.
do: **Automate** most of my own paperwork in the first few months.
Ask Kofi to train me on **site surveys**.
feel: Mostly **excited**, with a small **worry** in the background.
S1.quote: Someone will automate my paperwork, and I'd rather it was me, so I'm the one who understands it.
fieldNote: She moves **first**, automating her own job to stay in charge of it.
She worries more for an **older colleague** than for herself.
Her politics show up as **sharing gains**, not stopping the tech.

steps.text: Automate quotes, invoices and inbox sorting at SunPath
Ask Kofi for training on roof site surveys
Join the local campaign for green jobs training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for everyone, right now, because two years is nothing. I'd push for public money for people moving into hands-on trades. And I'd be loud about the AI companies paying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, the office part of my job is gone by 2028, whatever I do. Even the person who runs the AI tools isn't needed when the tools run themselves. The hands-on side of solar, getting panels on roofs, lasts until robots come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an electrician course straight away, evenings and weekends, and ask Kofi to put me on a crew as a trainee. My savings can cover a pay cut for well over a year. I'd keep using AI for everything at work until the last day, because it buys me time to train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but more fired up than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Only three years on the roofs before robots. Is that worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's three years of wages and a trade, which is more than nothing. And I'd guess robots on steep wet roofs take longer than the headlines say. I don't know that for sure, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the index fund payments, so I keep more cash. I wouldn't sell the fund, because if AI firms make huge profits, the fund owns a tiny bit of them. That's a strange thing for a left-wing person to say.

say: Two years is **nothing**, so we need a plan for everyone **right now**.
AI companies should **pay** for people moving into hands-on trades.
think: The **office part** of my job is gone by 2028, whatever I do.
Hands-on solar work lasts until robots arrive around **2031**.
do: Start an **electrician course** in evenings and weekends straight away.
Ask Kofi to put me on a crew as a **trainee**.
Pause **index fund** payments to hold more cash.
S2.quote: Even the person who runs the AI tools isn't needed when the tools run themselves.
fieldNote: She grasps that being **the AI person** stops protecting her under full AGI.
Her move is to **hands-on** work, accepting it only buys about three years.
Strong savings let her take a **trainee pay cut**.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening electrician course straight away
Ask Kofi for a trainee spot on an install crew
Pause index fund payments to keep more cash
Lobby for public money for workers moving into trades

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain a whole generation into trades, if we start now. I'd push for that locally. I'd be more hopeful than in the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is time to get fully qualified, not just a trainee. So in 2031, when the office work goes, I'd already be on roofs. Robots would come for that in 2034, and by then I'd be 35 with a trade and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the electrician course and keep running the office with AI. By year three I'd be splitting the week between office and crew. I might buy a share in SunPath if Kofi offered, since I'd know the business inside out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Focused. Like a training plan for a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you in 2034, when robots reach roofs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I won't pretend I do. Maybe I'd run the robots, or maybe I'd need a third career. I'd have savings and a few years to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a share sounds like a big step. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if machines do the work, owning a bit of the firm is how you still get paid. I'd want SunPath (the solar firm where she works) to be a co-op. The crews should own part too. Kofi might laugh at that.

say: Five years is enough to **retrain** a generation into trades if we **start now**.
I'd push for **local training** places and feel more hopeful.
think: I could be **fully qualified** before office work goes in 2031.
By **2034** I'd be 35, with a trade and savings.
do: Finish the **electrician course** in the first year.
Split my week between **office and crew** by year three.
Offer to buy a **share** in SunPath.
feel: **Focused**, like following a **training plan** for a race.
S3.quote: If machines do the work, owning a bit of the firm is how you still get paid. I'd want SunPath (the solar firm where she works) to be a co-op.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **plan in stages**: course, split week, ownership.
She is honest that **2034** is an open question.
Her politics reappear as wanting a **co-op**, with crews owning part.

steps.text: Finish the electrician qualification in the first year
Split the week between office and install crew
Offer to buy a share in SunPath as a co-op

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind. Free training, shorter weeks, a share of the profits for workers. I'd sound cheerful, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pretty relaxed. I'd use the first years to become the best AI-and-solar person around, and then shift into owning part of a firm. At 37, with ten years of savings and a trade, I'd be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, but start a small side business setting up AI admin for other installers. I'd do the electrician course over two or three years, no rush. And I'd keep investing every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little uneasy for people who won't start until year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you picture leaving it till year nine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maureen (who does the accounts part-time), probably, and half my school friends. Ten years feels long, so people relax. I'd try to nag my school friends early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the side business still make sense if AGI comes in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For about eight years it does, then probably not. That's fine, it's a bridge, not a forever plan. I'd save what it earns.

say: Ten years means **no excuse** for leaving anyone behind.
Workers deserve **free training** and a **share** of the profits.
think: I'd use the early years to become the best **AI-and-solar** person around.
At 37, with a **trade and savings**, I'd be okay.
do: Start a **side business** setting up AI admin for other installers.
Do the **electrician course** over two or three years.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a little **uneasy** for people who'll wait too long.
S4.quote: Ten years feels long, so people relax. I'd try to nag my school friends early.
fieldNote: She sees her **side business** as a bridge, not forever.
Her worry here is about **other people**, not herself.
Savings plus an early start make her one of the **calm** ones.

steps.text: Set up AI admin systems for other solar installers on the side
Complete the electrician course over three years
Keep monthly payments into the index fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be fine-ish, but lots of people wouldn't, and that worries me most. What would help is free trades training for anyone who wants it, paid for by the companies making money from AI.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they'd do with the time AI saves. I'd want shorter weeks, not more work.

headlineQuote: I'd keep using AI for everything at work until the last day, because it buys me time to train.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old** junior admin at SunPath, a twelve-person solar installer, who uses AI daily.
She has **over a year** saved through an index fund she started at 19.
She moves **first**, automating her own paperwork to stay in charge of it.
Under fast AGI she heads for an **electrician** trade, knowing robots follow three years later.
Her politics push for **shared gains**: shorter weeks, co-ops and free training.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, mainly for **other people** with less time and money.
whatWouldHelp: **Free trades training** for anyone, paid for by companies profiting from AI.
